The other reasons are control (you can't self-host it), compliance (where your prompts go) and logs. The short answer: LiteLLM if you want to self-host for free, Vercel AI Gateway if you want a hosted gateway with no fee at all, Cloudflare AI Gateway if you want caching and analytics on top of your own keys, and Opper if your data has to stay in the EU. If you're: paying OpenRouter's fee on a growing monthly bill, needing your own keys, logs and budgets per team, or shipping to customers who ask where their data goes, this list is for you. Most of what we handle comes as screenshots: a booking confirmation someone forwarded from WhatsApp, a flight reference, a payment receipt with an order ID. The prose on those screenshots is easy to read. The problem is the short codes, because a wrong code is worse than no code at all. I also maintain an OCR Actor on Apify, Image to Text . It runs Tesseract inside the container and returns the text, a page confidence and, if you ask, every word with its own confidence and pixel box. I wanted to know how far I could trust it on identifiers, so I made a test I could check against an exact answer.

articles.body: I wanted an image upscaler that runs entirely in the browser: no upload, no API key, works on a phone. This post covers what it took to get Real-ESRGAN running on ONNX Runtime Web with WebGPU and a WebAssembly fallback, and the few details that made the difference between "works on my laptop" and "works on any photo". The result is live at cv.cm/en/image-upscaler if you want to try it before reading. Picking a model that fits in a tab My first attempt used Swin2SR. Quality was fine, but on WebGPU it took seconds per 192 px tile . A 12-megapixel phone photo is a few hundred tiles, so that was a non-starter. Real-ESRGAN ships two "compact" models ( realesr-general-x4v3 for photos and realesr-animevideov3 for anime and line art) built on SRVGGNetCompact .

articles.title: When does Salesforce run Apex tests on a deployment, and how do you run fewer?

articles.body: Apex tests are the slowest part of most Salesforce deployments to production. This post explains when Salesforce runs them, which levels you can choose, the coverage rules that limit your options, and five practical ways to run fewer tests without breaking a deployment. The test levels A Metadata API deployment takes a test level. These are the ones the Salesforce CLI offers today: Level What runs NoTestRun No tests. RunSpecifiedTests Only the test classes you name. RunLocalTests Every test in your org except tests from installed managed packages. RunAllTestsInOrg Every test, including managed-package tests. RunRelevantTests Salesforce chooses tests based on the components in the package. A newer option that needs a recent API version (version 66 or later at the time of writing).

articles.title: Run Claude Code on a VPS and keep it running after you close the laptop
articles.excerpt: Short answer: install Claude Code on a Linux server and run it there, not on your laptop. Then it keeps working when the laptop sleeps. You can do this with plain tmux over SSH (below), or with SpaceA…
articles.body: Short answer: install Claude Code on a Linux server and run it there, not on your laptop. Then it keeps working when the laptop sleeps. You can do this with plain tmux over SSH (below), or with SpaceApp, which puts Claude Code and other CLIs in rooms you open from a browser. What is SpaceApp? SpaceApp is an MIT-licensed web app you run with Docker on your own machine or server. It replaces a wall of terminal windows with rooms: each room holds panes, and each pane is an AI coding CLI (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI and others), a copilot, a browser or a tool. The rooms live on the server, so the CLIs keep running when you close the browser tab or the laptop, and you open the same rooms from any browser. Every CLI runs on your own account.

articles.title: 12 grains of dust found high in Earth's atmosphere reveal secrets of water at the edge of the solar system
articles.excerpt: Grains of dust found floating in Earth's stratosphere hold the secrets of a special kind of 'heavy' water that seems to be abundant in the outer solar system.
articles.body: A dozen grains of dust that have wandered in from the distant Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune were found floating in Earth's stratosphere. And it turns out they hold the secrets of a special kind of 'heavy' water that seems to be surprisingly abundant in the outer solar system. When analyzed by a team of scientists the 12 dust grains, which were captured by NASA's stratospheric ER-2 research aircraft, show signs of having interacted with a form of water that contains heavy oxygen isotopes. This is important because to better understand how the planets formed, scientists are seeking to understand how various materials were distributed around the early solar system 4.5 billion years ago.
